#### Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in, with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.
A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
Each background task is known by its kind, from what started it: a subagent, started by an Agent or Task tool call, or a command, a shell command run in the background. Its start is when the harness said it had started, so how long it has been running can be told. A single background task can be stopped while the run goes on, without ending the run or any other task: the harness is asked, on the run's input, to stop that task by its id, Claude Code with its stream-json control request for stopping a task. The task then ends when the harness notifies its end, as ever, as stopped, and the harness carries on with what came of it. Stopping one is never done by stopping the harness's process, and a run whose input is already closed, or whose harness can't be fed, can't stop one on its own.
A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
A background command that never ends on its own, as a dev server started with `npm run dev`, `vite`, or `node server.js`, or a watcher, never keeps a task running once its work is done. Once a result has come, every message sent has been taken in, and no subagent is still going, a background command still running holds the run open only while it is busy: one that has printed nothing for 60 seconds since that result, as a server does once it has started and waits for requests, is taken as idle. Once every background task left is an idle command, the run asks the harness to stop each of them, as a single background task is stopped above, and once their ends are notified, the result that came is the run's last, and the task finishes in its state, done where it was. A command that keeps printing, as a long build or test run does, keeps the run open until it ends or goes quiet. While the run waits on background commands and nothing else, the task's status still reads "Running", and its tooltip says it is waiting on background commands, naming how many, which the subagents panel lists with their Stop buttons.
A harness's process that hasn't exited 10 seconds after the run's last result, with its input closed, as when a server it started still holds its output open, is ended with its whole process group, and the task finishes in the state of that last result, never left running. Whatever the run started is ended with it: no server a task started is left running once the task is shown as finished, so its port is free again.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

#### Description

It lists the background tasks the harness started for the run, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../../../scope/harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) keeps them: its subagents, the agents it started, and its background commands, the shell commands it ran in the background, such as a long build. A background task of any other kind isn't shown.
It is for what goes on apart from the run's main thread, so that while the main thread is waiting, paused, or has finished its turn, what is still going on is still seen. Every subagent is shown, whether the harness waits on it or runs it in the background. A command is shown only when it runs in the background, or when it runs long, as follows. An ordinary command the main thread waits on, a Bash tool call not run in the background, is never shown while it is short, and is shown only once it has been running for 15 seconds without its result coming back, from then until it ends, its time counting from its start as any row's does, its row taking its place among the others by when it started. A short command, done within those 15 seconds, never appears at all, not even for a moment, and neither does a command a subagent runs, which is part of that subagent's work, nor any other tool call. All of them are still rows of the task's output, as the [TaskTableScope](../../task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says; this panel only leaves them out.
A long command the main thread waits on isn't a background task: it doesn't hold the run open, and it ends when its tool call's result comes back, done or failed as that result says, or when the run ends, as the run did. Its tooltip's kind reads "Command, waited on". It has no Stop button, since the harness can stop only a background task on its own; the task's Cancel button stops it with the run.
A subagent the main thread waits on ends when the harness notifies its end, or else when its tool call's result comes back, whichever comes first, and can be stopped as a background one can wherever the harness gave it a task id, its Stop button left out otherwise.
It is shown only once the run has something to show in it, and takes no room before. One row per subagent or command shown, in the order they started, subagents and commands together, each 24 pixels tall, 8 pixels in from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is at work, then a tick, a cross, or a dash for how it ended, done, failed, or stopped, beside a small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a subagent that is its description, and for a command the command itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command", and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

#### Stopping

A row at work can be stopped, from a Stop button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, 18 pixels square, which takes the place of its running time while the row is hovered, whose tooltip reads "Stop this subagent" or "Stop this command". It lists the background tasks the harness started for the run, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../../../scope/harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) keeps them: its subagents, the agents it started, and its background commands, the shell commands it ran in the background, such as a long build. A background task of any other kind isn't shown.
It is for what goes on apart from the run's main thread, so that while the main thread is waiting, paused, or has finished its turn, what is still going on is still seen. Every subagent is shown, whether the harness waits on it or runs it in the background. A command is shown only when it runs in the background, or when it runs long, as follows. An ordinary command the main thread waits on, a Bash tool call not run in the background, is never shown while it is short, and is shown only once it has been running for 15 seconds without its result coming back, from then until it ends, its time counting from its start as any row's does, its row taking its place among the others by when it started. A short command, done within those 15 seconds, never appears at all, not even for a moment, and neither does a command a subagent runs, which is part of that subagent's work, nor any other tool call. All of them are still rows of the task's output, as the [TaskTableScope](../../task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says; this panel only leaves them out.
A long command the main thread waits on isn't a background task: it doesn't hold the run open, and it ends when its tool call's result comes back, done or failed as that result says, or when the run ends, as the run did. Its tooltip's kind reads "Command, waited on". It has no Stop button, since the harness can stop only a background task on its own; the task's Cancel button stops it with the run.
A subagent the main thread waits on ends when the harness notifies its end, or else when its tool call's result comes back, whichever comes first, and can be stopped as a background one can wherever the harness gave it a task id, its Stop button left out otherwise.
It is shown only once the run has something to show in it, and takes no room before. One row per subagent or command shown, in the order they started, subagents and commands together, each 24 pixels tall, 8 pixels in from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is at work, then a tick, a cross, or a dash for how it ended, done, failed, or stopped, beside a small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a subagent that is its description, and for a command the command itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command", and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

#### Stopping

A row at work can be stopped, from a Stop button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, 18 pixels square, which takes the place of its running time while the row is hovered, whose tooltip reads "Stop this subagent" or "Stop this command". content.content:
##### Stopping

Stopping a target stops everything it started, however deep: the shell its command runs in, what the shell runs, and every process those start in turn, as a `npm run dev` runs npm, which runs node, which runs Vite and its esbuild, or a `cargo run` runs the binary it built. A server a target starts, a dev server, a watcher, or anything listening on a port, is stopped with it, so its port is free once the target reads "Stopped", and running it again never fails for the port being taken by the run before. Nothing it started is left running, nor left behind as an orphan of the shell, whatever the platform.
So a target's command is started as the head of a process group of its own on macOS and Linux, a new session, and on Windows in a job object that every process it starts belongs to, its children's children included. Stopping it first asks the whole group or job to end, as Ctrl+C in a terminal would, SIGINT and then SIGTERM to the process group on macOS and Linux, and on Windows a Ctrl+Break to its console group, so a server can shut down cleanly; whatever is still running 3 seconds later is killed outright, SIGKILL to the group on macOS and Linux, and the job terminated on Windows. A process that left the group on its own, as one that starts a session of its own, is found among the target's descendants and stopped the same way.
The target reads "Stopped" only once every process it started has exited, and its Stop button shows a spinner and is disabled until then, so "Stopped" always means nothing of it is still running. Stopping it the other ways, by running another target in its place, finding the targets, closing its panel, or quitting, stops it just the same, and quitting doesn't leave a process of it running after Suspense has gone. A target that ends by itself, as when its command exits, leaves nothing it started running

###### Either

what is left of its group is stopped as above.

A target is over when its command's process exits, never only when its output closes: a server or other child that still holds the output open, after the command has exited, never keeps the target reading "Running". What it prints until then is still shown, and once the command has exited, the target reads "Exited with N" or its success, and what is left of it is stopped. A target whose command is the server itself keeps running, as it should, until stopped.

content.text:
I've changed the code so a task that starts a node/vite server finishes as Done instead of staying "Running" forever. All 536 tests pass (1 ignored) and clippy reports nothing new. I haven't run it against a real dev server. The Windows paths are only checked by reading them: a full Windows build fails here inside gpui.

**Why it got stuck:** the agent started the dev server as a background command, and any background command kept the task open until it ended. A server never ends. On top of that, Suspense read the harness's output until it closed, and a server can hold that output open after the harness has exited.

**Tasks** (`src/harness.rs`)
- **Spotting idle servers:** once the agent has given its result, every message sent has been taken in and no subagent is running, each background command's output file is watched. Claude Code names that file in the command's tool result. A command that prints nothing for 60 seconds after that result is idle.
- **Stopping them:** once only idle commands are left, Suspense asks Claude Code to stop each one by id. When they've all ended, the result that already came becomes the last one and the task finishes as Done. Anything the harness says after that is ignored.
- **Busy commands still count:** a build or test run that keeps printing keeps the task open until it ends or goes quiet.
- **10-second exit timeout:** output is now read on its own thread, so the run checks the harness every 250 ms even while nothing arrives. If the harness hasn't exited 10 seconds after its last result, its process group is asked to end, then killed 3 seconds later. The task then finishes with that last result.
- **Harness exited, output still held open:** the run finishes about a second later rather than waiting for the output to close.
- **Cleanup:** whatever is left of the harness's process group is ended when the run finishes, so the server's port is free.

**Status tooltip** (`src/subagents.rs`, `src/prompt_mode.rs`): while a task waits on background commands and nothing else, its "Running" status has a tooltip reading "Waiting on N background commands". Those commands already appear in the subagents panel with Stop buttons.

**Run targets:** nothing new was needed. The previous step already ends a target when its command exits, gives its output a second, then stops whatever is left. That step's test covers it.

**Tests added:**
- The idle rules: a quiet command is stopped once, then the last result is given; one still printing, a running subagent or an unanswered message keeps the task open.
- A fake harness that exits while a background `sleep` holds its output open: the run finishes and the `sleep` is killed.
- The "waiting on N" count.

**Where it falls short of the spec:**
- **Container runs:** the command's output file is inside the container's `/tmp`, which Suspense can't read from outside. So a background command in a Spec task is never treated as idle and keeps the task open. The 10-second timeout still applies once a last result has come. This was my choice; the spec doesn't cover it.
- **Windows:** the harness has no process group there. A server that outlives the harness no longer keeps the task running, but it isn't killed either.
- **Untested:** the 10-second timeout itself has no test, because it would add about 13 seconds to the suite.

The spec and your prompt didn't disagree. The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791386926-NodeServerStuckRunning2.understanding.md`.
